steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper on using LLM-generated pseudo data to tackle low-resource molecule discovery (translating between molecules and natural language descriptions). Motivate the problem, explain why paired data is scarce, introduce our pseudo dataset and how we use it, and end with a bulleted contributions list.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Molecule discovery is critical in many scientific domains, including chemistry, pharmacology, and materials science. But traditional methods for designing molecules often have problems like high costs, long development processes, and limited success rates. For example, bringing a new drug to the market might need over a billion dollars and more than a decade of development.

With the arrival of artificial intelligence (AI), new cross-modal methods are giving new ways to synthesize and analyze complex molecular structures, which improves efficiency and is reshaping computational chemistry and material science. Prior work proposed a new approach that directly translates molecules to their captions and generates molecular structures from natural language text, as shown in Figure 1. This cross-modal method points to a future where specialized molecules can be designed and studied just by using simple natural language sentences.

There have been various attempts at these tasks. MolT5 uses SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) and molecule descriptions separately for masked language modeling (MLM) as pre-training. Another work pre-trains models with causal language modeling (CLM) on sequences that mix biomedical literature with molecular structural representations, which they get by replacing molecular entities with their SMILES representations. But these studies are limited because parallel molecule-description pairs are scarce, so direct sequence-to-sequence training is not feasible. Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) training is clearly effective, as seen in other work where annotated data from the downstream dataset is included in pre-training, although at a much lower ratio than the unannotated data. The main bottleneck is the annotation process: annotating these pairs needs specialized knowledge of molecular chemistry, so large-scale human annotation is expensive and difficult.

LLMs have had great success in natural language processing (NLP) and related fields, and inspired by this we propose to deal with the low-resource problem by using artificially-real data that is generated by LLMs. "Real data" comes from genuine experimental or observational sources, but this "pseudo data" or "artificially-real data" is made artificially. It looks like real data in format, but its content does not describe actual real-world observations, so it may not be suitable for direct real-world applications.

- Approach
  - pseudo dataset for seq2seq pre-training
  - 1M unlabeled molecules from PubChem; LLM in-context learning -> captions
  - retrieval-based one-shot prompting for integrity, diversity
  - PseudoMD-1M: first artificially-real dataset, 1,020,139 pairs
  - two methods: pseudo data only in pre-training (domain adaptation); pseudo + real in fine-tuning (data augmentation)
  - DrugBank-23: new dataset, different data source
- Contributions
  - first to use LLMs for low-resource molecule discovery; mitigate data scarcity; release PseudoMD-1M, 33 \times larger than existing real datasets
  - construction and utilization of pseudo data: domain adaptation, data augmentation; experiments on existing datasets; DrugBank-23
  - results: smaller model, less pre-training data, domain adaptation beats all prior methods; continuous improvement with more pseudo data

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Molecule discovery is critical in many scientific domains, including chemistry, pharmacology, and materials science. But traditional methods for designing molecules often have problems like high costs, long development processes, and limited success rates. For example, bringing a new drug to the market might need over a billion dollars and more than a decade of development.

With the arrival of artificial intelligence (AI), new cross-modal methods are giving new ways to synthesize and analyze complex molecular structures, which improves efficiency and is reshaping computational chemistry and material science. Prior work proposed a new approach that directly translates molecules to their captions and generates molecular structures from natural language text, as shown in Figure 1. This cross-modal method points to a future where specialized molecules can be designed and studied just by using simple natural language sentences.

There have been various attempts at these tasks. MolT5 uses SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) and molecule descriptions separately for masked language modeling (MLM) as pre-training. Another work pre-trains models with causal language modeling (CLM) on sequences that mix biomedical literature with molecular structural representations, which they get by replacing molecular entities with their SMILES representations. But these studies are limited because parallel molecule-description pairs are scarce, so direct sequence-to-sequence training is not feasible. Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) training is clearly effective, as seen in other work where annotated data from the downstream dataset is included in pre-training, although at a much lower ratio than the unannotated data. The main bottleneck is the annotation process: annotating these pairs needs specialized knowledge of molecular chemistry, so large-scale human annotation is expensive and difficult.

LLMs have had great success in natural language processing (NLP) and related fields, and inspired by this we propose to deal with the low-resource problem by using artificially-real data that is generated by LLMs. "Real data" comes from genuine experimental or observational sources, but this "pseudo data" or "artificially-real data" is made artificially. It looks like real data in format, but its content does not describe actual real-world observations, so it may not be suitable for direct real-world applications.

Our approach starts by creating a large pseudo dataset for seq2seq pre-training. We collect 1M unlabeled molecules from PubChem and use the in-context learning ability of LLMs to generate descriptive captions for them. To keep the pseudo data sound and diverse, we use a retrieval-based one-shot prompting strategy during generation. This way we construct the first artificially-real dataset, PseudoMD-1M, which has 1,020,139 pseudo molecule-description pairs.

Using this dataset, we look for the best way to use pseudo data. We propose two main methods: 1) using pseudo data only during pre-training for domain adaptation, and 2) mixing pseudo data with real data during fine-tuning as data augmentation. To make the evaluation comprehensive, we also compile DrugBank-23, a new dataset that comes from a different data source than the existing datasets.

To sum up, our contributions are:

- • We are the first to use LLMs for low-resource molecule discovery. With artificially-real data generated by LLMs, we can mitigate the data scarcity for these tasks. We release PseudoMD-1M, the first artificially-real dataset for cross-modal molecule discovery, which is 33 \times larger than existing real datasets.

- • We explore how to construct and use pseudo data effectively. We look at two main techniques, using pseudo data as domain adaptation and as data augmentation. We run comprehensive experiments on existing datasets, and we provide a new dataset, DrugBank-23, which adds a new data source compared to the current datasets.

- • Experiments show that models using artificially-real data as domain adaptation outperform all prior methods, even though they have a smaller model size and less pre-training data. Also, our method keeps improving as the amount of pseudo data increases, which shows it has promising future applications.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Molecule discovery plays a critical role in many scientific domains, including chemistry [1,2], pharmacology [3,4], and materials science [5]. However, traditional molecule design methods often face challenges such as high costs, lengthy development processes, and limited success rates. Introducing a new drug to the market, for instance, may require over a billion dollars and more than a decade of development [6].

With the advent of artificial intelligence (AI), innovative cross-modal methods are opening new ways to synthesize and analyze complex molecular structures, improving efficiency and reshaping the fields of computational chemistry and material science. [7] proposed a novel approach that directly translates molecules to corresponding captions and generates molecular structures from natural language text, as shown in Figure 1. This cross-modal method points toward a future in which specialized molecules can be designed and studied through simple natural language sentences.

Various attempts have been made to address these tasks. MolT5 [7] uses SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) [8] and molecule descriptions separately for masked language modeling (MLM) [9] as pre-training. [10] pre-train models with causal language modeling (CLM) on sequences that blend biomedical literature with molecular structural representations, obtained by replacing molecular entities with their SMILES representations. However, these studies are limited by the scarcity of parallel molecule-description pairs, which makes direct sequence-to-sequence training unfeasible. The effectiveness of sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) training is evident in [11], where annotated data from the downstream dataset is incorporated into pre-training, albeit at a much lower ratio than the unannotated data. The primary bottleneck is the annotation process itself: annotating these pairs demands specialized knowledge in molecular chemistry, making large-scale human annotation both expensive and difficult.

Inspired by the great success of LLMs in natural language processing (NLP) and related fields [12,13,14], we propose to mitigate the low-resource difficulty with artificially-real data generated by LLMs. Unlike "real data", which comes from genuine experimental or observational sources, this "pseudo data" or "artificially-real data" is crafted artificially. It mirrors the format of real data, but its content does not depict actual real-world observations, which may make it unsuitable for direct real-world applications.

Our approach begins by creating a comprehensive pseudo dataset for seq2seq pre-training. We collect 1M unlabeled molecules from PubChem and use the in-context learning ability of LLMs to generate descriptive captions for them. To ensure the integrity and diversity of the pseudo data, we adopt a retrieval-based one-shot prompting strategy during generation. In this way, we construct the first artificially-real dataset, PseudoMD-1M, which consists of 1,020,139 pseudo molecule-description pairs.

Based on this dataset, we explore the best way to leverage pseudo data, proposing two primary methods: 1) using pseudo data exclusively during pre-training for domain adaptation, and 2) combining pseudo data with real data during fine-tuning as a data augmentation technique. For a comprehensive evaluation, we also compile DrugBank-23, a new dataset derived from a different data source than existing datasets.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- • We are the first to incorporate LLMs for low-resource molecule discovery. Using artificially-real data generated by LLMs, we mitigate the data scarcity for these tasks. We release PseudoMD-1M, the first artificially-real dataset for cross-modal molecule discovery, which is 33 \times larger than existing real datasets.

- • We explore the effective construction and utilization of pseudo data, investigating two principal techniques: pseudo data as domain adaptation and as data augmentation. We conduct comprehensive experiments on existing datasets and provide a new dataset, DrugBank-23, which adds a novel data source compared to current datasets.

- • Experimental results show that, despite a smaller model size and less pre-training data, models using artificially-real data as domain adaptation outperform all prior methods. Moreover, our method improves continuously as the volume of pseudo data grows, underscoring its promise for future applications.
